newsitem.title: CANADA: Fall in Canada's jobless rate spurs markets.
newsitem.headline: Fall in Canada's jobless rate spurs markets.

text.p: Canada's unemployment rate has finally made a significant downward move, setting off a rally in the Canadian dollar and fixed income markets, analysts said.
The June unemployment rate fell to 9.1 percent from 9.5 percent in May -- the lowest rate since September 1995, Statistics Canada said on Friday.
Job creation totalled 51,500 bringing the number of jobs in Canada to 13.95 million.

The strong report has been long awaited. While other indicators of Canada's economic health have been strong in recent months, the jobless rate has hovered stubbornly around 10 percent, damaging consumer confidence.

"I think the word 'tremendous' is an understatement," said David Rosenberg, senior economist at brokerage Nesbitt Burns in Toronto, referring to the latest jobless data. "This is the final piece of the puzzle and it's fitting into place quite nicely."
The Canadian dollar opened much stronger at C$1.3689 (US$0.7305) on Friday from Thursday's close of C$1.3733 (US$0.7282).
T-bill yields also moved higher following the report, with the yield on the 3-month-when-issued T-bill rising to 3.16 percent from 3.14 percent at Thursday's close.
Strength in the job market in June was broad-based, both regionally and across sectors, Rosenberg pointed out.
"We're packing quite a powerful punch here," he said.

Statistics Canada noted that the 51,500 rise in employment was accompanied by a decline of about 57,000 in the number of people looking for work, which pushed the unemployment rate down to 0.1 percent.
Full time employment rose by 93,700 from the month before, while part time employment fell by 42,200.
In the past four months, about 235,000 full-time jobs have been created, Statistics Canada said.

"That's more than the previous 28 months combined," observed Rosenberg, adding that the job market shows momentum that may prompt the Bank of Canada to tighten monetary conditions "sooner rather than later."

"I think the bank will likely take a pre-emptive strike," he said. The timing of the central bank's actions will likely depend on how much monetary conditions are tightened by a strengthening Canadian dollar, he added.
The Bank of Canada raised interest rates by a quarter of a percentage point last month, after more than a year of easing monetary conditions.
